title: Dedicated capacity buying guide for platform architects
content:
Purpose
This is a buyer-oriented guide and sales-facing playbook aimed at platform architects and procurement teams evaluating Redwood Dedicated capacity. Goal: make it easy for technical buyers to map business requirements (isolation, predictable throughput, latency SLOs, compliance) to procurement language, measurable SLAs, and negotiation levers.

Audience
- Primary: platform architects, infra/ML platform leads, procurement managers in enterprise accounts.
- Secondary: solutions engineers, AE, legal procurement reviewers.

Executive positioning (one-liner)
Choose Redwood Dedicated when you need cloud-like flexibility with enterprise-grade isolation and predictable inference economics — backed by SLA commitments and operational controls your platform team can trust.

Core buyer pillars (how to talk to architects)
1) Predictable throughput + capacity guarantees
   - What they care about: sustained qps/throughput for peak windows, consistent p95/p99 token latency at given sequence lengths, and ability to scale predictably without noisy neighbors.
   - Redwood answer: Reserved GPU pools sized to throughput commitments, configurable autoscale/burst policies, and capacity reservation primitives that map directly to throughput SLAs. Include sample: “X reserved GPUs -> Y concurrent requests for model M at 512 tokens, p95 latency <= 120ms.”

2) Strong isolation and data control
   - What they care about: no co-tenancy on inference nodes, network-level controls, VPC peering and private control plane, KMS integration, and audit trails.
   - Redwood answer: Dedicated tenancy option (no multi-tenant pods on same GPUs), optional private deployment with customer-managed networking, HSM/KMS key wrapping, and per-request audit metadata that can be forwarded to customer SIEM.

3) Measurable SLAs and operational playbooks
   - What they care about: clear uptime, latency, and throughput SLOs, plus fallbacks and compensation language for incidents.
   - Redwood answer: SLA buckets for Dedicated with uptime % (monthly), p95 latency windows, and throughput floor guarantees. Provide runbooks for failover (regional reroute, model degrade to smaller variant).

4) Cost predictability and unit economics
   - What they care about: predictable $/token or $/inference cost at scale, avoidance of hidden egress or burst charges, and procurement-friendly metering.
   - Redwood answer: Committed monthly pricing for reserved capacity, transparent unit rates for overages, and tooling to surface token-level cost breakdowns per route.

Architect-level artifact: capacity->SLA mapping matrix
(Example language for SOW / contract insert)
- Capacity Block: RBW-DED-XL (16x A100-equivalent GPUs)
- Guaranteed throughput: 8000 tokens/sec sustained at 512 token average request size
- Latency target: p95 <= 160 ms for 512-token sequences during single-region operation
- Availability: 99.95% monthly uptime for control plane & inference runtime
- Compensation: Service credit tiers tied to downtime windows and latency breach windows

Sample procurement-ready clause (short)
"Supplier will provide Dedicated Capacity (Capacity Block identifier RBW-DED-XL) that guarantees sustained inference throughput of 8k tokens/sec at an average request length of 512 tokens per request. Supplier will maintain p95 generation latency of <= 160ms under the guaranteed throughput and 99.95% monthly uptime. If Supplier fails to meet these commitments, Customer will be eligible for service credits as defined in Appendix A."

Negotiation levers to surface (for AE/SE)
- Burst buffer vs sustained commit: trade higher sustained commit for lower per-token price, allow limited free burst capacity for seasonal spikes.
- Observability retention: longer retention windows for tracing/metrics can be upsold; include sample retention tiers in SOW.
- Cross-region DR: offer warm standby region at reduced cost vs full active-active.
- Model quantization/optimizer support: recommended profiles that lower GPU cost with small quality delta; can be an implementation deliverable in the SOW.

Competitive notes (quick takeaways for sales conversations)
- Hyperscalers (AWS/GCP/Azure): Strong on procurement familiarity and network + identity integrations; weaker on turnkey model performance tuning and inference-focused batching optimizations. Hyperscalers often expect customers to manage model tuning and runtime. Redwood differentiator: inference runtime optimizations + turnkey capacity reservations with ML-centric SLAs.
- Open model API providers (OpenAI-like): Easy API but no guaranteed isolation or dedicated capacity with enterprise-grade network controls. More SaaS-like; Redwood offers the same developer ergonomics with isolation and SLA guarantees.
- Inference infra vendors / self-hosted stacks: Offer deeper control but require substantial ops lift. Redwood differentiates by operating the runtime (or delivering it as a private package) plus strong support and SRE runbooks.

Common procurement objections and rebuttals
- Objection: "We prefer on-premise for compliance."
  Rebuttal: Redwood Private supports on-prem and air-gapped options; we also offer hybrid private control plane with customer-managed keys.
- Objection: "How do we trust throughput numbers?"
  Rebuttal: Provide benchmark runs on customer-like trace, a short proof-of-capacity pilot, and explicit capacity mapping in the SOW.
- Objection: "What happens in an incident?"
  Rebuttal: We ship runbooks with the contract, agreed RTO/RPO for model-serving, and automated regional reroute policies; include escalation matrix with named SRE contacts.

Sales enablement checklist (what SE needs to bring to buying committee)
- Short tech brief for platform architects (this doc + model-specific throughput table)
- Example capacity sizing worksheet populated with customer token distribution
- Proof-of-capacity runbook template and pilot checklist
- Legal-friendly SLA language snippet + compensation table
- Pricing scenarios: base commit, commit+burst, and overage model

RFP / questionnaire starter (items procurement will ask for)
- Describe isolation model: physical GPU tenancy? tenant-aware scheduling?
- Provide historical uptime and incident summaries for the past 12 months
- Confirm KMS/HSM integrations and key custody model
- What telemetry and logs are accessible to the customer and for how long?
- Describe breach and compensation policy for missed SLA targets

Quick ROI example (narrative)
Customer: B2B SaaS with 100M tokens/day average usage.
- On shared-hosted pricing this is unpredictable and subject to noisy neighbors, leading to spikes and poor tail latency impacting UX.
- With a 12-month reserved Dedicated commitment, customer trades higher fixed cost for 40% predictable reduction in per-token operational variability, 15% lower effective latency (better UX), and improved developer velocity because platform teams no longer chase runtime incidents.

Next steps and asks
- For AE: collect 7-day token histogram and peak qps target from customer
- For SE: run a short capacity pilot (2–3 days) using the customer trace and capture p95/p99 latency at target commit
- For Legal: prepare SLA appendix template for inclusion in order form

Appendix: short sample metrics to capture during pilot
- Sustained tokens/sec (1h, 4h, 24h windows)
- p50/p95/p99 latency for generation at 128/512/1024 token lengths
- GPU utilization (per device) and batch size distribution
- Error rate and root-cause tags (timeouts, OOM, infra transient)

Notes to self / open items
- Validate exact GPU-equivalent mapping for RBW-DED-XL SKU with infra team (Marcus)
- Prepare standard SLO language options (3 tiers) for pricing page
- Create a one-page diagram showing Dedicated -> Private -> Hosted routing fallbacks for customer playbooks
